title: ScatterWorks: A Python package for building and solving scattering network models
authors: R. Johanna Zijderveld, Hélène Spring, Anton R. Akhmerov
abstract: Network models provide an efficient framework for studying non-interacting transport and wave-propagation phenomena in disordered and topological systems. We introduce ScatterWorks, an open-source Python package for building and solving network models. The package uses a compact network representation with composable transformation operations (tile, cut, relink, and union) to enable flexible construction of periodic and finite networks. Local scattering matrices on nodes can be assigned by node labels or explicit indexing, assembled into global scattering equations, and used to compute quasienergies and transport observables. The package supports sparse scattering matrices, allowing transport observables to be evaluated with Schur-based solvers. We demonstrate the package workflow on a symbolic Fabry-Perot interferometer and a numerical Chalker-Coddington model, recovering analytical expressions and the expected near-critical transport behavior of the quantum Hall transition. Plotting utilities with label-aware rendering are included to streamline debugging and reproducible setup for larger, custom network geometries.
summary: This paper introduces ScatterWorks, an open-source Python package designed to model and solve quantum transport problems in complex network geometries. It allows researchers to build systems using modular operations and calculate key observables like conductance and quasienergies. This tool is particularly valuable for studying disordered and topological systems where analytical solutions are intractable.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for a flexible and unified computational framework to study non-interacting transport and wave-propagation phenomena in complex, disordered, and topological quantum systems.
main_result: The authors introduce ScatterWorks, a Python package that successfully models and solves transport problems for systems like the Chalker-Coddington model, recovering expected critical behavior.
method: The package builds networks using composable transformations (tile, cut, union) and assembles local scattering matrices into a global scattering operator, which is then solved using Schur-based linear algebra techniques.
model_or_system: The models studied are general scattering networks, applicable to disordered systems, topological insulators, and moiré lattices. Examples include the Fabry-Perot interferometer and the Chalker-Coddington model describing the quantum Hall transition.
key_observables: Quasienergies, conductance (G), effective scattering matrix (S_eff), transmission (t), and reflection (r) coefficients.
important_parameters: The critical point parameter ($	heta_c = \pi/4$) for the quantum Hall transition, and the system size ($L$) governing computational scaling.
main_assumptions: The derivation of the effective scattering matrix assumes that the internal scattering block ($\mathbf{S}_{	ext{bb}}$) does not have an eigenvalue of one, preventing singularity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of the global scattering matrix, the basic setup of a Fabry-Perot interferometer, and the tiled structure of the Chalker-Coddington network, showing conductance vs. disorder parameter.
paper_structure: The paper details a systematic workflow: defining the base network, modifying it using operations (tile, cut, union, relink), compiling the global scattering operator, and finally solving for transport observables using Schur complements.
why_interesting: The package provides a powerful, general-purpose tool for calculating transport properties in complex quantum structures, which is highly relevant for studying open quantum systems and mesoscopic physics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Tiny basic network described by Eq. 2: (a) shows the link labels, and (b) indicates which scattering elements correspond to each link connection.
Figure 2: The basic network setup with node and link labels of the Fabry-Perot interferometer. We omit the node labels of the boundary nodes at the sides, because they are only used for bookkeeping.

Figure 3: Panels (a) and (b) present the unit cell and tiled Chalker–Coddington network, respectively, while panel (c) gives the eigenphases of the unit-cell scattering operator at zero momentum as a function of θ. The two eigenphase branches touch at θ = π/4.

Figure 3(c) shows that the energy bands cross at θ = π/4. This is the critical point of the Chalker-Coddington model, because at this value the probability of scattering to the left is equal to the probability of scattering to the right [1, 16, 27]. Far away from this critical θc the network is in a deeply localized phase, while near θc the localization length is determined by the symmetry class.

Figure 4: Conductance and runtime scaling in the Chalker–Coddington model. Panel (a) plots the disorder-median conductance versus θ near θc = π/4 for different system sizes L; the shaded regions span the 16th–84th percentiles across 50 disorder realizations. The conductance peaks as expected near θ = π/4 at about 0.5 e2/h. Panel (b) plots the mean runtime versus L on log–log axes; the error bars show the standard deviation over 50 random seeds and all values of θ, and the dotted O(L3) line is a reference guide.
